Final selection: An expert panel will assess the final proposals using four criteria: Transformative Ambition, Viability, Evidence of Results, and Durability. The winners will be announced in autumn 2027.

Growing reliance on private philanthropy

Billionaire Michael Moritz and his wife, artist Harriet Heyman, are offering up to $150 million for ideas that could improve life in San Francisco, launching a global competition to address the city's housing affordability crisis and post-pandemic economic decline.The open competition, called "Boundless San Francisco," was announced on Wednesday by Crankstart, the private family foundation run by Moritz and Heyman. Up to three winning organisations will receive between $10 million and $50 million each to carry out their proposals, according to an official statement from the foundation and reporting by Bloomberg.Any organisation from anywhere in the world can submit a proposal, regardless of the topic, as long as the project directly benefits San Francisco residents."The best ideas rarely come from where you expect them," Moritz, 71, said in an emailed statement.Organisers are running the competition with Lever for Change, a non-profit organisation that connects philanthropists with community projects. Lever for Change has previously managed large funding competitions, including grants to help revive South Side Chicago and expand mental health services across Texas, overseeing more than $2.6 billion in awards to date.Crankstart Chief Executive Officer Missy Narula said the global competition reflects the high-risk, high-reward approach used in venture capital investing. Moritz, a former Sequoia Capital partner born in Wales and knighted in 2013, built his fortune by investing in technology companies such as Google, YouTube and PayPal Holdings Inc.The competition will follow a multi-stage review process before the final funding is awarded:San Francisco has increasingly relied on private funding from wealthy residents to fill gaps in public services. Mayor Daniel Lurie, a former non-profit executive and Levi Strauss heir, has often worked with local technology and finance leaders to secure private support for public projects, including downtown events funded by cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen.Moritz has lived in San Francisco for more than 40 years and has given significant funding to local projects. Bloomberg calculations based on public records show Crankstart has donated more than $1 billion to regional non-profits, academic scholarships, art museums and healthcare providers since 2020.In June, Crankstart pledged $9.2 million to tackle illegal waste dumping in nearby Oakland after local voters rejected a tax measure that would have paid for cleanup crews.Moritz has also supported the San Francisco Standard local news site, funded political ballot measures, and invested in California Forever, a project aimed at building a planned city in Solano County near the Bay Area.
Article Summary: Billionaire Michael Moritz and his wife, artist Harriet Heyman, are offering up to $150 million for ideas that could improve life in San Francisco. The open competition, called "Boundless San Francisco," was announced on Wednesday by Crankstart, the private family foundation. Up to three winning organisations will receive between $10 million and $50 million each to carry out their proposals.

Article Title: 'More like humiliation than rejection': Indian PSU employee denied US tourist visa in 20 seconds, says never going to apply again
Article Text:
A government employee shared his experience of a US tourist visa denial in under 20 seconds at the Chennai consulate. (AI photo)

Canada visa denial

Does Canada visa denial lead to US visa denial too?

A 36-year-old Indian man, a government employee, shared his experience of US tourist visa refusal and explained why it felt more like a humiliation than rejection. The Redditor had to spend a lot of money to travel for biometrics and an interview and was disheartened that all went to waste in 20 seconds. While many Indians are getting rejected because they can't show enough ties to India to allay visa officers' concerns that they might not return to India, the Redditor, in his defense, has a government job in India which he said he has been doing for 14 years. It is not possible for government employees to overstay their visa in any other country as it would be immediately flagged.But as he laid out the case details and the questions that he was asked, Redditors pointed out why his visa was denied.The man said he was single and had no history of international travel. His interview at the Chennai consulate was short and he was asked the usual questions and also about the purpose of the intended visit, his employment, monthly salary and history of international travel."I know no travel history was the reason of rejection. Waiting for appointments, travel for biometrics, interview, book flight tickets, hotel booking, spending lot of money, getting formally dressed up only to get refused.It was more like humiliation than rejection. Never going to apply again," the man wrote.The Redditor also shared that his visa for Canada was also rejected but at least it was an easier process with fewer steps and only visa fee. He said he applied for visas for both the US and Canada on the same day but since the waiting time for a Canada visa is much shorter, the interview was done two months ago and he said he was told that he did not submit some additional documents.Redditors said that his Canada visa denial played the most significant role in his US visa denial as Canada and the US share immigration data because of their Five Eyes alliance. His fate was decided even before he walked up for the interview, Redditors said, suggesting that the man should travel to some European or Asian countries first before reapplying for either a US or Canada visa.A denial for a Canadian tourist visa does not automatically mean that a US tourist visa (B1/B2) will be denied. However, it does increase the likelihood of scrutiny and raises your risk of denial if the underlying reasons for the Canadian refusal apply to the US as well.The US and Canada share immigration and biometric data under the Five Eyes alliance (along with the UK, Australia, and New Zealand). The US consular officer will likely know about the applicant's Canadian refusal before the interview.Both nations look at the same core requirements: ties to home country, financial capability, and authenticity of travel purpose.
Article Summary: A 36-year-old Indian man, a government employee, shared his experience of US tourist visa refusal. The Redditor had to spend a lot of money to travel for biometrics and an interview and was disheartened that all went to waste in 20 seconds. Redditors pointed out why his visa was denied.

Article Title: One Houston man began clearing illegally dumped trash alone; his daily cleanups grew into a 100-volunteer movement
Article Text:
Andrew Beaver who runs “Clean the Block” removes debris with other volunteers

Building momentum online and on foot

Municipal limits and district hot teams

Legal enforcement and surveillance in Harris County

What started as one man's effort to clear dumped furniture and rubbish in south Houston has grown into a 100-person volunteer campaign to clean up historically underserved neighbourhoods.Andrew Beaver, 37, began clearing abandoned lots and alleyways in November without any experience running an organisation. Today, his nonprofit Clean the Block organises group cleanups across neighbourhoods like Sunnyside and Third Ward, filling hire trucks with illegally dumped waste."I grew up thinking, ‘Trash is disgusting. Someone should do something about it,’" said Beaver, a real estate investor who manages local properties. "But I’m in this area, I invest here, and if it’s giving so much to me, I wanted to find a way to give back."As reported Houston Chronicle, a recent Sunday cleanup in Sunnyside brought together about 100 volunteers. Armed with walkie-talkies and heavy gloves, participants cleared narrow alleyways, nearby streets, creeks and vacant lots while listening to music from portable speakers.The Sunday cleanup gained support through a partnership with Sole Ties Run Club, a local running group that combines fitness with community service.Robel Yemane, co-founder and president of Sole Ties, said social media posts showing Beaver's daily cleanups helped attract an unusually large crowd.“You’re more likely to impact the community you live in by pouring back into the people,” said Yemane. “You have all these beautiful homes, and when there’s trash everywhere, it makes people feel like the neighborhood isn’t being served properly.”The social media campaign turned online followers into volunteers. Emma Kremowski, 25, joined after seeing the project on Instagram.“I’m a big fan of community initiatives,” Kremowski said. “It’s hard not to be involved in some way with everything going on. We’ve got to show that we care.”For residents living near places where rubbish is regularly dumped, the community effort is making a real difference. Emily Wroczynski, a Third Ward resident, said people often dump trash in empty lots.“It feels like you’re doing something that actually makes a difference,” Wroczynski added about her decision to volunteer.Community groups often step in when city services cannot keep up. In neighbourhoods like Sunnyside and Third Ward, residents say abandoned rubbish is often left untouched for weeks or even months.Coordinating waste removal between volunteers and local authorities was difficult at first, but communication with city officials has improved. A spokesperson for Houston City Council District D confirmed that council staff met with Beaver, with more meetings planned to improve coordination.The district office provides logistical support and sends "hot teams" to remove large amounts of rubbish. District officials also encourage residents to report illegal dumping through the city's 311 system and share tracking numbers directly with district staff.Paying for these municipal hot teams requires significant funding. Previous Houston Chronicle reporting showed that council districts spend between $61,000 and $175,000 each year from district service funds on specialised cleanup crews. City officials say these costs are due to budget constraints and staff shortages within Houston’s Solid Waste Management Department.Along with city cleanup efforts, law enforcement agencies are increasing efforts to catch people who dump waste illegally.Harris County Precinct 7 Constable James “Smokie” Phillips said his office relies on public tip-offs, extra patrols and hidden cameras to investigate cases.“When we get a call, we follow up,” Constable Phillips said. “If we have good information, we’ll do an investigation and pursue charges through the District Attorney’s Office.”Phillips said illegal dumping blocks drainage systems, attracts pests and damages the appearance of neighbourhoods. His office is still seeking funding to expand camera surveillance in problem areas, noting that investigations at night require a lot of time and effort.Under the Texas Health and Safety Code, dumping waste anywhere other than an approved solid waste site is illegal. Depending on the amount of waste and whether it is a repeat offence, penalties range from criminal misdemeanours to state jail felonies for large-scale commercial dumping. Municipal programmes like Houston's One Clean Houston Initiative also use surveillance footage to investigate and prosecute offenders.Despite administrative and legal challenges, Beaver plans to continue his daily work.“It doesn’t take much to make me feel like this is working,” Beaver said. “We had 10 people once, and I thought that was crazy. Now people are truly showing up.”
Article Summary: Andrew Beaver, 37, began clearing abandoned lots and alleyways in November without any experience running an organisation. Today, his nonprofit Clean the Block organises group cleanups across neighbourhoods like Sunnyside and Third Ward, filling hire trucks with illegally dumped waste.

Article Title: 'There needs to be accountability': UN warns Pakistan over crackdown on peaceful PoK protesters
Article Text:
Pakistan's widening crackdown in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) draws international attention. (Photo: ANI)

The United Nations has warned Pakistan and called for accountability for any action taken against people participating in peaceful protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK). This came amid continuing unrest and concerns over restrictions on public gatherings and internet access, a spokesperson for UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres said.Asked whether the UN would seek accountability for the reported crackdown on protesters, deputy spokesman for the secretary-general Farhan Haq said authorities must ensure that people are allowed to exercise their right to peaceful protest.“It’s important that all authorities everywhere allow for peaceful protest, and certainly that is the case here. If there have been people harmed for engaging in peaceful protest, there needs to be accountability for that,” Haq told PTI.“The Secretary-General supports the work of his high commissioner, and we certainly hope that the pleas made by Mr Turk will be listened to,” he added.UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Turk had last month expressed concern over the escalating unrest in PoK and called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations into deaths among both protesters and security personnel.According to the UN, dozens of people, mostly protesters but also members of the law enforcement agencies, had reportedly been killed since June as tensions rose ahead of elections to the legislative assembly.Turk had also called for calm and urged authorities to address the underlying grievances of the local population through meaningful and inclusive political dialogue.The UN human rights chief further criticised Pakistan’s decision to ban the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and arrest some of its leaders.The JAAC, a coalition of traders, transporters, students, lawyers, activists and other groups, has been leading protests over political and economic issues in the region.The UN also raised concerns over restrictions on internet access and public gatherings, warning that such measures could undermine the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.“We urge the authorities to ensure full Internet access throughout the territory,” the UN statement said.The comments from the UN come amid heightened tensions in PoK, where protests and violence have also disrupted the regional election process.The JAAC has alleged that more than 40 people were killed during the first phase of polling on July 27 and has claimed that around 400 protesters have been killed since the first week of June. The Pakistan government has rejected the figures as “overly exaggerated”.“The number of people killed in the protests is in two digits. Moreover, security personnel have also lost their lives,” Pakistan Prime Minister’s adviser Rana Sanaullah said in a recent television interview.The unrest has also affected the election process in PoK. Authorities on Friday postponed voting indefinitely in seven of the 11 constituencies scheduled to vote in the third phase on August 10, citing concerns over the law-and-order situation. The first two phases of polling, held on July 27 and August 2, were marred by violent protests and allegations of rigging.
Article Summary: The United Nations has warned Pakistan and called for accountability for any action taken against people participating in peaceful protests. This came amid continuing unrest and concerns over restrictions on public gatherings and internet access. UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Turk had last month expressed concern over the escalating unrest in PoK.

Article Title: Unknown gunmen kill Pakistani policeman, abduct another in separate incidents
Article Text:
The motive behind both the incidents could not immediately be ascertained.

A police constable was shot dead and another was abducted in two separate attacks in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, officials said on Thursday.The incidents took place late on Wednesday night in Bannu and Tank districts. Police said the motive behind the attacks remains unclear and investigations are under way.In the first incident, Constable Noor Alam, who served in the Special Branch, was killed after unidentified gunmen opened fire on him while he was travelling from his home to report for duty in Bannu district.According to police, Alam regularly used the same route to reach his workplace. He was attacked near Masoomabad on the Bannu-Miranshah Road within the jurisdiction of Cantt Police Station. The assailants fled immediately after carrying out the shooting.In a separate incident, Constable Irfanullah, a wireless operator posted at Shaheed Mureed Akbar Police Station, was abducted from his native village of Sheikh Awtar in Tank district while he was on leave.District Police Officer, Tank, said a search operation had been launched and an investigation into the abduction was underway, adding that efforts were being made to ensure the safe recovery of the abducted constable.
Article Summary: The incidents took place late on Wednesday night in Bannu and Tank districts. Police said the motive behind the attacks remains unclear and investigations are under way. In the first incident, Constable Noor Alam was killed after unidentified gunmen opened fire on him while he was travelling from his home.

Article Title: Pakistan's crackdown in PoK: How Islamabad is tightening information chokehold amid global scrutiny
Article Text:
Pakistan imposes strict restrictions on media (ANI photo)

Pakistan's widening crackdown in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) has drawn international attention, with members of the Kashmiri diaspora, rights groups and global watchdogs raising concerns over restrictions on journalists and media freedom.The measures, introduced by the Shehbaz Sharif government during the so-called assembly elections in the illegally-occupied Valley, have also been criticised by press freedom organisations.According to The New York Times, Pakistan has imposed strict rules requiring journalists working for foreign media outlets to seek government permission before travelling outside Islamabad, Karachi and Lahore.The restrictions come amid increased media coverage of protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, where demonstrators have been demanding greater political autonomy since early June.The NYT reported that the restrictions could severely affect independent reporting from Pakistan."Heavy local journalists say will close off one of the last remaining ways to get independent journalism about the world’s fifth-most-populous country," the report said.Pakistan has also ordered journalists working for foreign media organisations to leave PoK immediately."The requirement that journalists obtain state approval to report from large parts of the country sends a chilling message: that critical reporting is unwelcome," Pakistan’s leading human rights organisation said in a statement.Journalists covering developments in PoK have come under particular pressure. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), two independent Pakistani journalists were detained on August 1 and taken to an undisclosed location.Several others have reportedly been summoned to court under a law that criminalises "false and fake information" over their reporting from the region.The new restrictions have also been criticised internationally. Patricia Gossman, Human Rights Watch’s senior associate Asia director, called them an "alarming step in the country’s narrowing space for press freedom and free expression." Pakistan ranks 153rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders Press Freedom Index.The Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists also urged the Sharif-led government to withdraw the restrictions. "If the government is really interested in showing that it believes in democracy and press freedom, then it should immediately lift this ban," the organisation said.Pakistan's ministry of information, however, said foreign media organisations would continue to operate normally and that the government was working on a new system for issuing travel permits.The restrictions are expected to have the biggest impact on reporting from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, where the election process is scheduled to conclude on August 10.The region has witnessed months of protests demanding constitutional reforms, while authorities accuse protesters of violence and demonstrators accuse security forces of suppressing peaceful protests.According to local officials and independent estimates cited by the NYT, at least 30 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July.Meanwhile, India has also strongly condemned the neighbouring Pakistan's crackdown on PoK. The ministry of external affairs called the local elections as "a complete farce." The MEA also highlighted the situation gripped with violence, blackouts, intimidation, and repression against civilians.The Kashmiri diaspora abroad has also staged a strong demonstration in UK. The agitated people took to the streets of Bradford, condemning Pakistan's crackdown in PoK.
Article Summary: Pakistan imposes strict restrictions on media. Restrictions come amid increased media coverage of protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Kashmiri diaspora abroad has staged a strong demonstration in UK. India has also strongly condemned the neighbouring Pakistan's crackdown on PoK.

Article Title: Imran Khan's three years in jail spark protests across Pakistan; over 100 held
Article Text:
More than 100 supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan have been arrested as rallies were held across Pakistan on Wednesday to mark the completion of three years of his imprisonment.

Peshawar rally sets September 27 deadline

Family, PTI leaders raise detention concerns

Over 100 supporters of jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan were arrested on Wednesday as Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters held rallies nationwide to mark three years of his imprisonment. The demonstrations, which called for Khan’s release, saw police fire tear gas at protesters in Rawalpindi amid clashes and heightened security.The main rally was held in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where PTI is in power. The party demanded Khan’s release and restoration of his rights. Thousands of supporters gathered amid heavy security, according to Al Jazeera.In Punjab, Police baton-charged protesters and arresting scores of PTI workers in Lahore, Mianwali and Rawalpindi. In Lahore's Mall Road, police dispersed demonstrators demanding Khan's release and detained several protesters.Video footage circulated on social media showed rapid response force (RRF) using force against demonstrators. Some journalists covering the rally were also allegedly thrashed by police, prompting protests from media bodies.PTI Punjab general secretary Chaudhry Bilal Ejaz said five party lawmakers were among 25 others arrested in Lahore.“Despite this era of oppression, repression, and fascism, a large number of PTI workers and office-bearers in Punjab staged protest rallies and pledged to stand with Imran Khan,” he told news agency PTI.According to PTI, at least 50 workers were arrested in Mianwali, Rawalpindi and other parts of Punjab. In Karachi, police used tear gas to disperse PTI supporters protesting in Saddar Town and arrested more than 10 demonstrators. The party also claimed six workers were arrested in Pano Aqil and 15 in Kandhkot.On Wednesday, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Muhammad Suhail Afridi announced that PTI supporters will march towards Islamabad on September 27 if 'justice' is not provided to Khan.Addressing supporters in Peshawar, Afridi said the party's first demand was for cases against Khan and his wife to be heard and decided on merit. Its second demand, he said, was restoration of meetings with their legal team, doctors, relatives and party leaders.He claimed that if justice is delivered, Khan can be released “within 30 minutes”. Otherwise, he said, people from across Pakistan will march to Islamabad on September 27.Aleema Khan, sister of the ousted PM, said the movement for his release had already begun and its next phase would be announced soon.PTI senior leader Moonis Elahi alleged that Khan “has been denied meetings and proper medical treatment, and his eyesight has also deteriorated” in prison.Khan, 73, was arrested on August 5, 2023, and has remained in prison while facing multiple cases. His party has repeatedly alleged that the cases are politically motivated, a charge denied by the Shehbaz Sharif-led government.Amnesty International, a global non-governmental organization, also called on Pakistani authorities to uphold Khan's rights. Acting Regional Director for South Asia Isabelle Lassee said, “For three years, Pakistan’s authorities have systematically denied Imran Khan the right to a fair trial, subjected him to prolonged solitary confinement, and limited his access to medical care and visitation rights.”Lassee further said Khan had not been allowed to meet his family for more than eight months and that he and his wife, Bushra Bibi, had been denied regular access to legal counsel since December 2025.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters held rallies nationwide to mark three years of Imran Khan's imprisonment. The demonstrations, which called for Khan’s release, saw police fire tear gas at protesters in Rawalpindi amid clashes and heightened security. The main rally was held in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Article Title: Peace talks abroad, protests at home: The many contradictions shaping Pakistan today
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir (R) (PTI file photo)

From military confrontation to diplomatic outreach

The Iran gamble

A war next door, and Pakistan's opportunity

Living on lifelines, dreaming of leadership

Source: IMF

Security ambitions amid diplomatic outreach

Diplomacy abroad, discontent within

Operation Sindoor 's lasting fallout

Operation Sindoor fallout

Sites targeted during Op Sindoor

The Balochistan challenge refuses to fade

BLA

Pakistan's uneasy neighbourhood

Presence of TTP remains a major challenge for Pakistan

A nation seeking influence while confronting instability

"A house divided against itself cannot stand." Abraham Lincoln's observation aptly captures Pakistan 's situation.While Islamabad chases the image of an indispensable diplomatic player, its own foundations appear increasingly fragile. From brokering peace in Middle East to courting Washington and Beijing, Pakistan has sought a larger role in global diplomacy.Yet back home, it remains weighed down by economic distress, political unrest, separatist movements, water shortages, terrorism, and accusations of human rights abuses, an uneasy contradiction that defines the country's present-day reality.Much of Pakistan's strategic direction continues to be shaped by its military establishment, with army chief Asim Munir, the country's de facto centre of power. His influence extends well beyond defence matters, as Pakistan's military continues to function as a parallel authority that heavily influences domestic governance as well as foreign policy.That contrast between projecting stability abroad and confronting instability at home, has become one of Pakistan's defining geopolitical challenges.Just over a year ago, Pakistan suffered one of its most difficult periods on the diplomatic and military fronts following India's response to the Pakistan-backed terror attack in South Kashmir's Pahalgam.New Delhi's "zero-tolerance" policy under Prime Minister Narendra Modi translated into a series of retaliatory actions that once again placed Pakistan under international scrutiny over terrorism.Yet, even as tensions with India remained elevated, Islamabad quickly sought to recast its international image.Already maintaining close ties with China, Pakistan simultaneously attempted to deepen engagement with Donald Trump's United States. For a country grappling with a fragile economy, maintaining goodwill with both Washington and Beijing has become increasingly important.It was in this backdrop that Pakistan pitched itself as a potential mediator between Iran and the United States.Pakistan's bid to position itself as a regional peace broker did not begin smoothly.Its initial attempt to host talks between Iran and the United States faltered after Tehran rejected Islamabad as the venue. According to The Wall Street Journal, Iran formally informed mediators that it would not attend the proposed talks with American officials in Pakistan.Islamabad, however, persisted.Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and military head Asim Munir stepped up engagement with Washington, with Munir's growing proximity to the Trump administration earning him the title of Trump's "favourite field marshal".Around the same time, Sharif attended President Xi Jinping 's grand military parade in Beijing alongside leaders including Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.The event reinforced Pakistan's continued strategic closeness with China even as it simultaneously sought stronger engagement with Washington.Six months later, the geopolitical landscape shifted dramatically as President Donald Trump launched military strikes against Iran, joined by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu under Operation Epic Fury.Global Shia icon and longest-ruling Supreme Leader of Iran Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed on the opening day of the offensive on February 28, 2026 in Pakistan's neighbourhood.The raging Tehran regime's response left the Middle East region totally disturbed. Bombs, missiles and drones fell, almost hitting every country in the region.Retaliatory strikes and military activity engulfed large parts of the region, with airspace disrupted across Iraq, Kuwait, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen, Oman, Jordan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.However, Pakistan, despite its border with Iran, remained untouched and safe.That made Islamabad a potential venue for talks with Iran's new leadership under Mojtaba Khamenei .Sensing an opportunity, Pakistan declared itself a peace broker. On April 8, Sharif posted on X announcing a ceasefire that actually wasn't close to peace.He wrote: "With the greatest humility, I am pleased to announce that the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States of America, along with their allies, have agreed to an immediate ceasefire everywhere including Lebanon and elsewhere, EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY."In May, army chief Asim Munir hailed the development as "slight progress". US Vice President JD Vance visited Pakistan twice for peace talks, but despite the diplomatic efforts, the fighting continued and a lasting peace remained elusive.Still, the symbolism was already disheartening. The same country where the US carried out Operation Neptune Spear to eliminate Osama bin Laden had now become Washington's chosen venue for talks with Iran.Islamabad may be eager to wear the badge of a global player, but its economic reality tells a far less flattering story. Beneath the grand diplomatic posturing lies a cash-strapped nation surviving on lifelines from China, the United States, the IMF and other international lenders, hardly the profile of a country calling the shots on the world stage.According to Reuters, the IMF in May completed reviews of its lending programmes with Pakistan, clearing the way for approximately $1.32 billion in fresh funding.The package included nearly $1.1 billion under the Extended Fund Facility and around $220 million under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility, taking total disbursements under the two ongoing programmes to roughly $4.8 billion.Pakistan remains under a $7-billion IMF programme after reaching a staff-level agreement in March."Amid a more challenging and highly uncertain external environment since the onset of the war in the Middle East, Pakistan needs to maintain strong macroeconomic policies while accelerating reform efforts," the IMF said in a statement.For Islamabad, therefore, diplomacy is not merely about regional influence. It is also about preserving the confidence of the international community at a time when its economy remains deeply dependent on external financing.Alongside its mediation efforts, Pakistan has also sought to deepen strategic partnerships within the Islamic world.Islamabad has moved closer to Turkey and Saudi Arabia, readying a Nato-style Islamic security arrangement with mutual defence provisions reminiscent to Nato.The defence pact, signed by Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in September, states that "any aggression" against one member would be treated as an attack on all , a provision that closely mirrors Nato's Article 5. Turkey, already a Nato member, fields the alliance's second-largest military after the United States.While the arrangement remains far from becoming a formal military alliance, it reflects Islamabad's broader effort to strengthen its regional security architecture to counter New Delhi.However, the economic and military size of the two-nuclear armed nations still remain widely different.Pakistan lagging far behind.Even with Islamabad's projected flamboyancy in foreign dealings, unrest continues across Pakistan and regions illegally occupied by Pakistan.The most visible flashpoint in recent months has been Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), where the so-called Assembly elections have been conducted in three phases amid allegations of police excesses and restrictions on dissent.Videos and reports emerging from the region have shown violent confrontations between security forces and protesters, prompting criticism from rights groups and attracting international attention.Pakistan's own defence minister, Khawaja Asif, further fuelled controversy with remarks defending the government's actions."I put the protesters of PoJK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Asif said.The statement reflected Islamabad's increasingly uncompromising approach towards dissent in the region.The ministry of external affairs strongly denounced Pakistan's mischievous handling of the situation, describing the elections in PoK as a "complete farce". The MEA also condemned the Islamabad-backed ill-treatment and crackdown that killed 90 people in the region since June this year.Human rights organisations have echoed similar concerns.Amnesty International USA called reports emerging from PoK's Rawalakot as "disturbing" and urged Pakistani authorities to restore communication services and permit independent media and observers into the region."The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities' long history of unlawful violence against protesters in PoJK. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty International USA posted on X.The developments have reinforced criticism that, while Islamabad attempts to mediate conflicts abroad, it continues to face accusations of suppressing dissent within territories under its own control.Behind the fancy overcoat of its foreign policy ambitions, Pakistan ultimately bore the brunt of its fertile terror fields it had long nurtured.The fallout from Operation Sindoor did not just damage Pakistan-backed terror camps and military infrastructure.India swiftly showcased the scale of its response, striking nine terror bases and 11 military installations across Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK).The consequences of Operation Sindoor extended beyond military targets to the country's most basic necessities, including water. With all major rivers in Pakistan flowing into its territory from India, New Delhi had placed the decades-old Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance immediately after the Pahalgam massacre of April 22, 2025.The country is facing an increasingly severe water crisis, particularly across Sindh and Balochistan , where shrinking river flows and uneven distribution have triggered alarm among farmers, political leaders and water experts.Months after New Delhi's decision, Pakistan is confronting growing concerns over agricultural losses, declining livelihoods and mounting economic pressure across several provinces.Sindh, home to Karachi, Pakistan's financial capital, has emerged as one of the worst-hit regions, with water shortages threatening agriculture and affecting millions of people.Prime Minister Narendra Modi had encapsulated India's position soon after the Pahalgam attack."Terror and talks cannot go together; water and blood cannot flow together," he had said.The message was reiterated recently by defence minister Rajnath Singh recently on Kargil Vijay Diwas."After the Pahalgam terror attack, by suspending the Indus Waters Treaty, we said that those whose tears have dried up should not expect water from us. We will not let the waters of the Sindhu reach the patrons of terrorists and enemies of humanity," Rajnath said.For Pakistan, the water crisis has added yet another layer to an already fragile economic and political situation, with experts warning that prolonged shortages could further aggravate regional discontent.While PoK has dominated headlines in recent weeks, Balochistan continues to represent Pakistan's longest-running internal security challenge.The province recently announced plans to observe its own Independence Day, underlining the persistence of separatist sentiment.The conflict, rooted in grievances dating back to Balochistan's accession to Pakistan in 1948, revolves around demands for greater political autonomy, control over natural resources and opposition to mega infrastructure projects such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).Over the decades, the conflict has been marked by armed insurgency, heavy militarisation and repeated allegations of human rights violations.Yet Balochistan is only one strand of Pakistan's broader internal unrest.The country's dissent is neither unified nor driven by a single cause.Separatist groups in Balochistan, the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, political activists and unemployed youth often pursue vastly different objectives.That fragmentation, however, has also worked to the advantage of Pakistan's establishment.Without a unified opposition, the state has been able to confront each movement differently, labelling one as terrorism, another as separatism, others as political disorder or foreign conspiracy.Rather than confronting a single nationwide challenge, Islamabad faces multiple disconnected crises, each requiring a different response.For neighbouring Iran, Pakistan has recently struck the chord of "peace", offering itself as a mediator, though the negotiations have yielded almost no progress.Its ties with Tehran, however, have rarely been straightforward. Relations with India remain frozen, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi making New Delhi's position unequivocal: "If there will be talks between India and Pakistan, it will only be on terrorism and PoK."To the west, Pakistan's troubles are no less daunting. Crossborder tensions with Taliban-ruled Afghanistan have intensified, even as Islamabad grapples with a surge in terror attacks at home.Beyond the long-running insurgency in Balochistan, Pakistan faces an increasingly potent threat from the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). While the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021, Islamabad's hopes of gaining strategic leverage quickly unraveled. Kabul has refused to dismantle TTP sanctuaries, allowing the outfit to regroup and intensify attacks across Pakistan.The fallout has been severe. Cross-border clashes have become more frequent, while the TTP, an umbrella militant group formed in 2007, continues to challenge the Pakistani state's authority, specifying the irony of a country seeking to broker peace abroad while battling an escalating insurgency at home.Pakistan today finds itself pursuing two parallel realities.On one hand, it is attempting to establish itself as a regional diplomatic player, offering to mediate conflicts, expanding defence partnerships and seeking greater geopolitical relevance.On the other, it continues to wrestle with economic fragility, dependence on IMF assistance, unrest in PoK and Balochistan, a worsening water crisis and an increasingly complex internal security landscape.Adding to these challenges is the country's continued struggle with terrorism. According to the Global Terrorism Index 2026, Pakistan ranked as the country most affected by terrorism, recording more than 1,000 terror-related deaths in 2025, its worst figures since 2013.For Islamabad, diplomatic visibility on the global stage may offer strategic dividends and international goodwill. But as long as domestic crises continue to deepen, Pakistan's ambitions abroad will remain overshadowed by the challenges it faces at home.
Article Summary: Pakistan has sought a larger role in global diplomacy. But back home, it remains weighed down by economic distress, political unrest, separatist movements, terrorism, and accusations of human rights abuses. The contrast between projecting stability abroad and confronting instability at home, has become one of Pakistan's defining geopolitical challenges.

Article Title: Hand grenade explosion kills 3 in northwest Pakistan
Article Text:
Police hints towards a family dispute

PESHAWAR: At least three people, including a woman and a child, were killed and three other children sustained injuries in a hand grenade blast in northwest Pakistan , police said on Wednesday.The incident occurred on Tuesday in the Bahram Khel area of Lakki Marwat district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.According to the police, a family dispute triggered the hand grenade explosion.All three deceased individuals and three injured children were taken to a nearby hospital, police said, adding that an investigation into the incident is underway.No case has been registered so far, police said.
Article Summary: The incident occurred on Tuesday in the Bahram Khel area of Lakki Marwat district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. According to the police, a family dispute triggered the hand grenade explosion. All three deceased individuals and three injured children were taken to a nearby hospital.

Article Title: NOC to travel outside Islamabad, Lahore, Karachi - Pakistan restricts foreign journalists amid PoK crackdown
Article Text:
Pakistan tightens curbs on foreign media (Reuters image)

Pakistan has imposed fresh restrictions on foreign media personnel, requiring journalists working for international news organisations to obtain a No Objection Certificate (NOC) before travelling outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi for reporting assignments.The new guidelines, issued by Pakistan's ministry of information and broadcasting (MoIB), establish a comprehensive framework governing the registration, accreditation and movement of foreign media organisations and journalists operating in the country.Under the rules, journalists are exempt from the No Objection Certificate (NOC) requirement when travelling within Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi. For personal travel to Abbottabad and Murree, they may apply for an NOC through the ministry's External Publicity (EP) Wing, with approvals expected within three working days.“All Pakistani journalists residing abroad, contributing to foreign media and seeking registration must submit their application through the EP Wing portal and concurrently forward their case through the nearest press attaché, counsellor, minister posted in Pakistan missions, consulates, high commissions, or embassies,” the MOIB said, as cited by Dawn.Additionally, the guidelines require all companies, entities, production houses and other organisations operating in Pakistan to facilitate foreign media "in any capacity" to register with the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting's publicity wing.The registration requirement also applies to non-journalists residing in Pakistan who provide services to foreign media organisations.The new rules apply to all international media organisations, including print, electronic and digital outlets, as well as web-based platforms and social media organisations.The regulations also require production houses, companies, freelancers, fixers and non-journalists providing services to foreign media in Pakistan to register with the ministry. It clarified that the registration is intended solely for professional recognition and does not grant any official status."All foreign/international media personnel already accredited or registered with EP Wing shall be required a mandatory NOC from EP Wing for movement to any other city (except Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi) in case they are going to produce a news content, story, video, film, documentary or social media content for their official use," the guidelines state.After completing the registration process, journalists seeking a press accreditation card must submit an application through the online portal along with the required documents. The guidelines provide for two categories of accreditation: permanent accreditation, issued annually, and temporary accreditation for visiting journalists, valid for up to three months.Once the external publicity wing issues the accreditation card, it will "facilitate" journalists' access to official media events and government premises.The guidelines state that journalists will be "bound to produce that card on demand", and must surrender it if they change their organisation or accreditation category, or when the accreditation period expires.The latest measures come amid heightened scrutiny of media access in Pakistan following reports of protests, disruptions and the alleged use of force during the local election process in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK).Human rights and press freedom organisations, including Amnesty International and Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), have raised concerns over alleged restrictions on journalists, communication blackouts, enforced disappearances of media personnel and curbs on foreign media coverage of the protests. Amnesty International has also called for an independent investigation into allegations of excessive force used against demonstrators in Rawalakot.
Article Summary: New guidelines establish framework governing registration, accreditation and movement of foreign media. Journalists exempt from NOC requirement when travelling within Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi. For personal travel to Abbottabad and Murree, they may apply for NOC through ministry's External Publicity (EP) Wing.

Article Title: Over 30 operatives killed by 'Indian agents' since 2020: LeT commander
Article Text:
Rizwan Hanif, a commander affiliated with Lashkar-e-Taiba, has alleged that Indian agents have systematically killed more than thirty individuals in different Pakistani locations since 2020. He characterized these murders as acts of religious persecution and rejected the authority of foreign entities. This statement comes amid heightened rhetoric from Pakistan's military, and experts suggest it serves as a strategic narrative amidst rising tensions.

In a significant public admission by terrorist organisation Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT), senior commander Rizwan Hanif has claimed that over 30 members linked to the group have been killed across Pakistani cities since 2020 by "India agents". LeT members were targeted in Peshawar, Karachi, Rawalpindi, Muzaffarabad and Rawalakot, Hanif said while addressing a crowd in Pakistan.Attempting to frame these targeted killings as religious persecution, Hanif - the wanted deputy chief of Lashkar's POK unit - launched into inflammatory rhetoric. In a video circulated on social media, he questioned the group's "crime", asserting they were targeted solely for their faith.Hanif also launched a sharp attack against other faiths in his speech which was filmed by his followers and uploaded on social media.He declared that the outfit would continue its activities, rejecting the authority of foreign powers, including the US and Israel.The hate-filled speech comes on the heels of Lt General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, the official spokesperson of Pakistan armed forces (DG-ISPR), and the son of a US-designated terrorist peddling similar extremist views on a video while alleging that Afghans were not Muslims.Security experts saw these speeches as a face-saving narrative building exercise. The escalation in sectarian rhetoric comes as Islamabad faces mounting public unrest in Pakistan-Occupied Kashmir, where violent state crackdowns against anti-govt protesters at Rawalakot, in particular, and other places have drawn severe criticism while denting Pakistan's narrative about it being the champion of Kashmiris and their right to self-determination.Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif also labelled anti-govt demonstrators in POK as "enemies" comparable to India and ruled out any dialogue with them while defending the violent attacks on protesters.
Article Summary: Rizwan Hanif, a commander affiliated with Lashkar-e-Taiba, has alleged that Indian agents have systematically killed more than thirty individuals in different Pakistani locations since 2020. He characterized these murders as acts of religious persecution and rejected the authority of foreign entities. Article Title: 'Long history of unlawful violence': Global watchdogs condemn Pakistan's crackdown in PoK
Article Text:
PoK (File photo)

As Pakistan-occupied Kashmir goes through its so-called assembly polls, reports of brutality, violence and unrest continue to surface, with global human rights and press freedom watchdogs raising alarm over an escalating crackdown on protesters and the media.International organisations, including Amnesty International and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), have flagged allegations of state-backed violence, restrictions on independent reporting, enforced disappearances of journalists and prolonged internet shutdowns. They have urged Pakistani authorities to end the crackdown, restore communication services and ensure transparent investigations into alleged human rights violations.Highlighting reports of excessive force used against demonstrators in Rawalakot, Amnesty International said the incidents reflected Pakistan's long record of using unlawful violence against protesters."The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities' long history of unlawful violence against protesters. A prompt, independent, and transparent investigation must be ordered into the security forces' use of force against protesters.So long as an internet and mobile services blackout remains in place, it will severely impede the independent verification of the full extent of the situation on the ground. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty said in a post on X.Echoing similar concerns, CPJ said it was monitoring the deteriorating press freedom situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, citing internet blackouts, telecommunications shutdowns, reporting restrictions and the detention and disappearance of journalists.The press freedom watchdog also expressed concern over the reported disappearance of independent journalist Razi Tahir and his colleague Muhammad Saif, who were allegedly taken by men in police uniforms from their office in Islamabad on August 1."CPJ is deeply concerned by reports that independent journalist Razi Tahir and his colleague Muhammad Saif have been missing since August 1. They were reportedly taken by men in police uniforms from their office in Islamabad, and their whereabouts remain unknown. Pakistani authorities must acknowledge whether they are in state custody, ensure due process, and immediately release them if they are being arbitrarily detained," it wrote.In a subsequent update, CPJ said the two journalists remain missing while Kashmiri journalist Raja Ikram, who was reportedly detained in Islamabad on August 1, has since been released."Journalists Razi Tahir and Muhmmad Saif remain missing after reportedly being taken by men in police uniform on August 1. Pakistani authorities must acknowledge their detention if they are in state custody, ensure due process, and immediately release them. Kashmiri journalist Raja Ikram, who was reportedly detained in Islamabad on August 1, was later released," it added.CPJ also said the media crackdown appears to be extending beyond the region, pointing to reported action against major news outlets alongside continuing telecommunications disruptions.The criticism comes as casualties continue to mount during the ongoing protest movement. According to figures released by the Human Rights Council of Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (HRC-PoJK) as of Sunday, at least 80 people have died, including 33 civilians before July 27, 43 people killed since July 27 across Rawalakot, Mirpur and Muzaffarabad, and four Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir police personnel.
Article Summary: Watchdogs raise alarm over escalating crackdown on protesters and the media. Amnesty International, Committee to Protect Journalists have flagged allegations of state-backed violence, restrictions on independent reporting and enforced disappearances of journalists. They have urged Pakistani authorities to end the crackdown, restore communication services and ensure transparent investigations.

Article Title: 'They'll arrest us at hospitals': PoK protesters risk death over electricity, flour demands
Article Text:
Dozens killed in PoK as protesters treating gunshot wounds in makeshift clinics avoid hospitals for fear of arrest

Makeshift clinic treats dozens of critically injured

JAAC and authorities trade accusations

Food shortages, roadblocks add to tensions

A protest movement in PoK has escalated into deadly clashes between security forces and demonstrators, with dozens of people reportedly killed across the region in recent weeks, the BBC reported.The protests have been led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding cheaper electricity and flour as well as better access to education, healthcare and other basic services. The movement says an agreement reached with the governments of Pakistan and PoK in October to address some of its demands has not been implemented.The BBC reported that Rawalakot, one of the main centres of the protests, was experiencing severe disruption, with roads blocked, shops shut and internet access cut off.The BBC visited a makeshift clinic near the main protest site, where a spare bedroom had been converted into a medical supply area and a bed placed outside beneath a tarpaulin was being used to treat injured protesters.A doctor identified by the BBC as Dr Anwar said the clinic had treated around 50 to 60 critically injured people since July 27, including an estimated 15 to 20 people with gunshot wounds.The doctor said the facility could provide basic emergency treatment, including stopping bleeding, dressing wounds and removing superficial bullets, but lacked the equipment required for serious injuries involving the chest, abdomen, head or other vital organs.He also said protesters were reluctant to seek treatment at the main hospital because of fears they could be arrested or shot there. Authorities have rejected that claim.The BBC spoke to families who said relatives had been shot during the protests. One woman, identified as Asma, said she was at a demonstration when she learned that her only son had been shot. Another man, Salman, told the BBC that his younger brother had died.The JAAC says its demonstrations are peaceful and focused on economic and basic-rights demands. The group has rejected allegations that it is responsible for violence, while authorities have accused it of being armed and attempting to disrupt ongoing elections in the region.The JAAC was banned in June and labelled foreign-funded terrorists by the authorities, according to the BBC. The group rejected the characterisation and said its financial support was from the PoK diaspora and not India, an accusation that Pakistan has tried to make on multiple occasions.Authorities have also accused the group of attacking law-enforcement personnel and obstructing public order. Officials have released drone footage that they said showed JAAC members carrying guns on rooftops and displayed weapons they said had been recovered from the group.The government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters, saying law-enforcement personnel acted against people involved in attacks on security forces, threats to public safety or obstruction of lawful authority.The JAAC, meanwhile, has alleged that security forces were responsible for firing on protesters. Umar Nazir, a member of the group's core committee, also alleged that people had infiltrated the movement and may have carried out violence to support the authorities' narrative, though he provided no evidence for the claim.The BBC said that during protests it attended, its journalists saw no weapons or shooting among demonstrators, although gunshots were heard overnight and it could not establish who was firing or at what.The unrest has also disrupted supplies in Rawalakot. The BBC reported seeing food shortages, with most shops closed and protesters sharing available food. Some residents described attempts to smuggle rice into the city.Several roads have been blocked by fallen trees and other debris. Authorities have blamed the JAAC for the blockades, while also denying that they were preventing food or medical supplies from reaching Rawalakot.The protests come as local elections are taking place in PoK, adding another layer of tension to the confrontation.
Article Summary: Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) has been demanding cheaper electricity and flour as well as better access to education, healthcare and other basic services. The BBC visited a makeshift clinic near the main protest site, where a spare bedroom had been converted into a medical supply area. A doctor said the clinic had treated around 50 to 60 critically injured people since July 27.

Article Title: '15-year-olds shot, only asked for basic rights': Inside the deadly PoK crackdown
Article Text:
Deadly clashes continue during protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir

'Most victims were 15 to 35'

'We are not terrorists'

Teenagers as young as 15 have been among those killed or seriously injured in a sweeping crackdown on protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), according to a report by the BBC based on the accounts of residents, doctors and families from the protest hub of Rawalakot. The demonstrations in Rawalakot by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) have turned deadly amid an ongoing security operation.The report said that dozens of people have been killed across the region over the past two months in clashes between security forces and protesters. The demonstrations comes as local elections are underway in the region.A doctor identified as Dr Anwar said that he had treated 50 to 60 critically injured patients since July 27, including 15 to 20 people with gunshot wounds."Most of those who have been killed or seriously injured are young people between about 15-16 years old and 32-35 years old. I have seen very few patients over the age of 40," BBC quoted the doctor saying.According to the report, many injured protesters have avoided government hospitals fearing arrest or being shot, a claim denied by the authorities.Families of those killed described the protests as a movement for basic rights, including affordable electricity, flour, education and healthcare."We only asked for affordable flour, electricity and our basic rights," Ali, whose friend Shafqat Hussain was fatally shot, told the BBC. "Instead, our brothers are being killed. What was our crime? Why are live bullets being fired at us?"Asma, whose only son was killed, said: "We were only asking for our rights. We are not terrorists." She added, "He knew there were risks, but he believed standing up for justice was important. He used to say that dying for a just cause was an honour."Another resident, Salman, whose younger brother died during the protests, told the BBC: "He was the youngest in the family and was loved by everyone... I feel proud that he gave his life while standing up for the rights of the people. He was not fighting or attacking anyone."The JAAC says the protests stem from the government's failure to implement an agreement signed in October that promised relief on electricity prices and other public welfare issues.The group, which was banned in June and designated by authorities as a foreign-funded terrorist organisation, denies the allegation, insisting it is a peaceful movement funded by the PoK diaspora.The Pakistan-occupied Kashmir government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters. It said law enforcement acted only against individuals involved in attacks on security personnel, threats to public safety or obstruction of lawful authority.
Article Summary: Dozens of people have been killed across the region over the past two months in clashes between security forces and protesters. The demonstrations in Rawalakot by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) have turned deadly amid an ongoing security operation. The Pakistan-occupied Kashmir government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters.

Article Title: 'Do not befriend Kaafirs': Pakistani general levels terror allegations against India
Article Text:
Pakistan's military spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry

Pakistan's military spokesperson, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, has sparked controversy after saying in a video that Muslims should not befriend "kaafirs" (non-believers), warning that those who do would no longer be considered among the faithful."Do not befriend kaafirs (non-believers) and leave the faithful. If you do that, there's a problem. Then you are not among the Muslims," Chaudhry said while addressing a press conference.“Now our population is 240-250 million people, and we still have four provinces. We have to see whether this is serving the purpose of good governance. That debate has to be sensibly held by politicians, by those in power, even those who have previously been in power, and those who are responsible to the people of Pakistan,” he added.The remarks were made during a wider media briefing that focused on Pakistan's counter-terrorism operations, the security situation in Balochistan, and the country's ties with Afghanistan.Taking a jibe at India-Afghanistan ties, Chaudhry claimed that the Afghan Taliban regime's "business" was terrorism, alleging that it used militancy to sustain its economy, state institutions and diplomacy.“Even their diplomacy is centred on terrorism. What is common between India and Afghanistan, except their DNA? The only thing common is terrorism,” Chaudhary said, as cited by Dawn.Chaudhry also claimed that around 300 Indian websites were being used to support terrorism-related activities in Balochistan, while more than 1,000 social media accounts and what he described as a "hostile diaspora" were involved in spreading propaganda linked to terrorism.“First, an event or incident is seeded, right or wrong, and then it is framed by initiators, who hand it over to amplifiers. Then mass amplification is done by mainstream Indian media, channels and their print media as well, from where it is picked up by international media, and then you take it and run it as facts," he said.The DG ISPR said the government was also working to strengthen the police force, including by deploying newly recruited assistant superintendents of police (ASPs) to Balochistan and providing bulletproof vehicles, among other measures.The remarks come amid a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces across Balochistan last month, with armed clashes also reported during military operations in the Mastung and Kech districts, according to The Balochistan Post (TBP).The insurgency in Balochistan has been led by several separatist groups, including the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), which has waged a long-running campaign against Pakistan's federal government. The group has frequently targeted security personnel and infrastructure in the province and has also carried out attacks in other parts of the country, including Karachi.According to Pakistan's 2023 census, Balochistan is home to around 15 million people and is rich in natural resources, including coal, gold, copper and natural gas. The BLA maintains that these resources should belong to the people of Balochistan and opposes the federal government's control over their extraction and the province's security.
Article Summary: Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Muslims should not befriend "kaafirs" (non-believers) He warned that those who do would no longer be considered among the faithful. The remarks were made during a wider media briefing on Pakistan's counter-terrorism operations.

Article Title: Pakistan restricts digital news websites reporting on PoK protests, crackdowns: Report
Article Text:
Pakistan expands online curbs following coverage of PoK unrest

Pakistan has reportedly expanded digital censorship measures by restricting access to several news websites following extensive media coverage of the ongoing unrest in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK).Alongside the reported blocking of local and regional news websites, international broadcasters, have also become inaccessible to users in parts of Pakistan, according to media reports cited by ANI.The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK). Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions.The channels facing possible blocking include those linked to Pakistan's main opposition party, its leader and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, as well as several journalists critical of the government, according to a court order dated June 24.Earlier in July, Al Jazeera reported that a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad had ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels based on a June 2 report by Pakistan's National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA).The agency alleged that the channels had published content that was "intimidating", "provocative" and "derogatory" towards state institutions and public officials.Al Jazeera reported that digital rights groups have warned the proposed bans could further restrict freedom of expression in Pakistan. With television and print media facing significant curbs, social media remains one of the few platforms for public debate and dissent, the report said.The broadcaster also reported that YouTube had notified 27 content creators that their channels could be blocked if they failed to comply with the court's directives.The restrictions come amid heightened sensitivity over the flow of information related to the political situation and local protests in PoK.The second phase of elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) was marred by widespread disruptions, logistical challenges and continuing protests, raising fresh concerns over the credibility of the electoral process.Polling was held across 21 constituencies, including nine in the Muzaffarabad Division of PoK and 12 refugee constituencies located in different parts of Pakistan.Voting was disrupted in several constituencies as road blockades and protests affected access to polling stations and delayed the electoral process.
Article Summary: Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions. The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) Earlier in July, a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels.

Article Title: Clarify Dhaka policy: Bangladesh to India after Hasina’s presser

India itself has to decide what their foreign policy will be regarding Bangladesh. We want good relations, in the interest of the people of both countries,” she said. “But the relationship has to be based on equality, with mutual respect and maintaining their own interests. If India understands that, it will be good for everyone,” she said.

Article Title: B’desh student party leaders accuse Hasina of trying to create unrest from Indian soil
Article Text:
Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, center, looks at an exhibit at the inauguration of a museum which will serve as a memorial for those killed during the mass uprisings in July 2024, at the former residence of Bangladesh's ousted leader Sheikh Hasina, in Dhaka, Bangladesh, on Wednesday

Dehradun:

National Citizen Party, formed by student leaders who led the anti-Sheikh Hasina mass movement in 2024, has accused the ousted former Bangladesh PM of trying to create unrest in the country from Indian soil after she declared at a news conference in New Delhi that she would return in Dec.Ariful Islam Adeeb, senior joint convener of NCP, told TOI from Dhaka on Thursday that Hasina and Awami League had lost political relevance after she fled Bangladesh, and that her latest remarks were aimed at disturbing the situation back home. “After fleeing the country, she and her party, Awami League, have become politically insignificant. Now, by making such statements from India, she is not just trying to create unrest but also ruining bilateral relations between the two countries,” Adeeb said.The reaction came a day after Bangladesh’s ministry of foreign affairs issued a strongly worded statement condemning Hasina’s media interaction in New Delhi. “Bangladesh is outraged that the absconding convicted genocider Sheikh Hasina was allowed this evening to engage in live interaction with the media in New Delhi where she and her henchmen launched venomous vitriol against Bangladesh and her people,” the ministry said.NCP, founded after the July Uprising that forced Hasina from power, said her remarks were also an attempt to put pressure on the elected govt by creating the possibility of a law-and-order situation through her supporters who remained in hiding. “Hasina is convicted for mass atrocities and killings during her 15 years of rule. Now, she is trying to put pressure on a democratically elected govt by keeping it on its toes to tackle possible law-and-order problems that may be created by her supporters. But NCP, like every other citizen of Bangladesh, will never allow that to happen,” Adeeb said.Bangladesh MFA also said Hasina’s interaction had come on the second anniversary of the July Revolution, calling it an insult to those who died during the uprising. “On a day when the people of Bangladesh are observing the second anniversary of the July Revolution, this interaction by Sheikh Hasina on Indian soil stands as an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh and a grievous insult to the martyrs of July Revolution,” the statement said.While NCP and Hasina’s other political rivals described her as politically irrelevant, some independent observers said Awami League and its former leader still remained central to Bangladesh’s political calculations. Md Saiful Alam Chowdhury, associate professor in the department of mass communication and journalism at University of Dhaka, said Hasina’s possible return could alter the political mood.“Hasina is the elephant in the room, which nobody wants back in the country. Every political rival, including ruling BNP, knows very well that the day she returns to Bangladesh, there will be tremors in the political scenario. The very evidence of it is the reaction from govt and parties to her decision to return,” Chowdhury said.He added that Hasina’s return would put smaller parties and even the ruling formation under pressure. “Parties like NCP and Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami will exist only on paper if she returns. BNP will also become vulnerable as Hasina will hog the limelight in the media and on the international stage. As of now, the country can only wait and watch her next actions,” Chowdhury said.
Article Summary: National Citizen Party, formed by student leaders who led the anti-Sheikh Hasina mass movement in 2024, has accused the ousted former Bangladesh PM of trying to create unrest in the country. Ariful Islam Adeeb, senior joint convener of NCP, told TOI from Dhaka on Thursday that Hasina and Awami League had lost political relevance.

Article Title: Bangladesh Chalo: Defiant Hasina says will return, not afraid of jail or death
Article Text:
Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina announced that she will return to her country

Holding her first public press conference since her ouster exactly two years ago, former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina reiterated her determination to return to her country by the end of this year. Addressing virtually the media gathering in Delhi, Hasina provided her version of events that led her to flee Bangladesh. She asserted that a conspiracy had been hatched to misguide genuine students, who protested against her govt, leading to its dissolution.Highlighting the violent character of the 2024 upheaval, Hasina said that hundreds of offices belonging to her Awami League party were vandalised, houses of Awami leaders were burnt, policemen attacked and killed, and thousands of Awami supporters were assaulted and murdered. Yet, the Muhammad Yunus-led interim govt passed an indemnity ordinance, later converted into a law, to protect the violent protesters.“I, myself, had instituted a judicial inquiry commission to investigate all the cases of violence independently, so that the truth could be known. But after the Yunus regime seized power, they stopped the work of the commission. If they had nothing to hide, why would they prevent the inquiry?” said Hasina.Alleging continuing violence and persecution under the current BNP-led govt, Hasina said that at least 10,000 Awami leaders and workers have been killed or disappeared. “Many Awami leaders, intellectuals and workers also continue to languish in jail without due process or trial, and they have been subjected to torture and denial of their legal rights.”Hasina’s son and senior Awami leader, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, who also joined the press conference virtually from the US, stressed on the indemnity point. “None of the police killings, per the indemnity law, can be prosecuted. So, my question is this: Are killings acceptable? If you can have blanket immunity for protesters who killed police officers, killed civilians and Awami League members and leaders, then why blame anybody?”Joy added, “Bangladesh today is a failed state. There are no human rights, there is no freedom of speech. Political killings in Bangladesh, since August 2024, have been legalised.”Hasina also laid down her demands. “The ban on the Awami League must be lifted, political prisoners must be released, false cases must be dropped, freedom of speech must be restored, media freedom must be protected, and judicial independence must be guaranteed.” Asked about her return and the currentBangladeshi govt’s intention to arrest her if she does so, Hasina asserted, “I have been arrested many times in my political life. After returning to Bangladesh in 1981, I was arrested in 1983. Then again in 1985, 1987, even in 2007 they tried to stop my return when I was outside Bangladesh. But I returned. I know they might arrest me or even kill me. But my people support me and I have to be with them to save Bangladesh. I will not let fear dictate my life. ”
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina announced that she will return to her country by the end of this year. She said that a conspiracy had been hatched to misguide genuine students. Hasina said that at least 10,000 Awami leaders and workers have been killed or disappeared.

Article Title: 'Why December? She should come now': Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman's aide challenges Sheikh Hasina
Article Text:
Rahman's aide challenges Hasina

A day after former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina , in a virtual press conference, announced that she would return to the country in December despite the risk of arrest or imprisonment. Bangladeshi system and Bangladeshi judiciary, Bangladesh administration, and Bangladeshi people's opinion will decide whether she will be welcomed or whether she will go to jail," Alal said.His remarks came after Hasina, in her first virtual press briefing since being ousted during the student-led uprising in August 2024, announced that she planned to return to Bangladesh in December despite the possible consequences."Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people. Article Title: Video shows petrol bomb attack on Shakib Al Hasan’s home after Hasina’s Delhi presser
Article Text:
A petrol bomb was reportedly hurled at Shakib Al Hasan’s ancestral home in Magura after he joined Hasina’s Delhi presser.

The house of former Bangladesh cricket captain Shakib Al Hasan in Magura was attacked on Wednesday evening, hours after he appeared virtually at a media interaction addressed by ousted former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina from Delhi.The incident took place at around 8:45 pm local time at Shakib's ancestral residence in the Keshabmor area of Magura town. Police and local sources said unidentified people vandalised the house, threw bricks and stones and attempted to set it on fire.Local reports said a petrol bomb was hurled at the upper portion of the iron gate on the southern side of the property.Several windows were reportedly shattered during the attack, while no injuries were reported. Police personnel were deployed outside the residence following the incident.The attack came hours after Shakib, a former Awami League MP from the Magura-1 constituency, participated in a virtual media interaction organised by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia in New Delhi.During the interaction, Hasina defended her government's handling of the July-August 2024 unrest and said the student-led uprising that led to her ouster was a “meticulously designed” regime-change operation rather than a spontaneous protest.Hasina also said “organised groups” had hijacked the protests and turned them into “instruments of violent political agitation”. She claimed the movement was used to “create a path to power outside ballot box.”The Awami League alleged the attack was linked to Shakib's participation in the event, saying, “Torching residences : the cost of attending Awami League press conference. Neo fascism engulfs Bangladesh.”Police have not identified the attackers or established a motive. The investigation is expected to determine whether a petrol bomb was used and who was behind the assault.
Article Summary: A petrol bomb was hurled at Shakib Al Hasan's ancestral home in Magura. The attack came hours after he appeared virtually at a media interaction addressed by ousted former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina from Delhi. Police and local sources said unidentified people vandalised the house.
